Why Tim Cook is wrong: A privacy advocate's view

There is no "backdoor" involved here. What appears to be involved is a design flaw. Something about the iPhone 5C in question is broken. Either it is possible to load a compromised firmware into the phone despite the fact that the phone is locked, or it is possible to read the data off the flash chips and attack it in a VM until the password is brute-forced.

Or perhaps it isn't possible, the judge isn't informed enough on the topic to know that it isn't possible, and Apple is painting the situation as a broader issue rather than stating on the narrow scale that they literally cannot do it.

As far as I am concerned, the judge is in the right here. Apple is not being ordered to create a flaw and distribute it to all devices. It is not being prevented from fixing this flaw in future devices. It is being asked to exploit a flaw that currently exists, and for the privacy-conscious this is actually a good thing.

So let's follow this train of thought. What happens when another cop confiscates an iPhone. Can they also send it off to Apple to have the secret sauce rubbed on it so that they can brute force the password to get the data? It's the same thing that happened in this case, so why not? More over, why not just force Apple to create a handy dandy program that will do this for the police? Did he not think this through? Jesus.

Just because Apple has thorough understanding of the file system on the iPhone and probably has tools that would be capable of circumventing the screen lock to modify the OS in ways that would render the screen lock useless or otherwise cracked without compromising the data doesn't mean that it's obligated to do so at the whim of any government investigation that comes its way. The person who owned that phone has a (continued) reasonable expectation of privacy. The lock screen and failed attempt wiping aspects of it are features designed to ensure that privacy.

The warrant is immaterial. Is it illegal to have a device that would destroy potentially incriminating evidence if your house is infiltrated by an untrained hand? The ten strike wipe mechanism is something along those lines.
In the case of having a warrant for materials on the device, I think yes.
